title: Versions, not translations
hookLine: many popular "Hafiz" poems in English are modern inventions, not translations
tomorrow: what do people do at Hafiz's grave in Shiraz?

lines: WHAT DOES THE REAL ONE SOUND LIKE?
cards: Inés sends Zoe the perfect line for the invitation, signed Hafiz: a gentle one about the sun never asking the earth to pay it back. It's all over her feed.
Zoe goes looking for it in an English Hafiz that follows the Persian, and comes up empty. The line comes from a popular modern book of versions, new poems written in Hafiz's spirit.
Readers of Persian can't match some of them to anything in his Divan. So what does the real Hafiz sound like?

teach.h: SAMARKAND AND BUKHARA, FOR A MOLE.
teach.b: Like this. In one of his well-known ghazals, he says: if that Turk from Shiraz would take my heart in hand, for the black mole on her cheek I'd give away Samarkand and Bukhara. Two great cities, for a mole.
And a legend grew around that line.
The conqueror Timur takes Shiraz and summons the poet. I conquered much of the world to adorn Samarkand and Bukhara, he says, and you'd give them away for a mole?
Hafiz, in a patched cloak, bows: it's by such generosity, sire, that I've come to this poverty. Timur laughs and sends him off with a gift. Historians doubt the two ever met.

teach.h: THE REAL HAFIZ: SPECIFIC AND RISKY.
teach.b: But notice what the real Hafiz is like: specific, cheeky, risky, Persian to the bone, full of his city and his Quran. The versions are softer. They sound like comfort with a well-known name attached.
Here's how his readers keep him. Hafiz is a book a culture keeps: memorized, opened on the longest night, recited at his tomb.

teach.h: A LINE IS HIS IF IT'S IN THE DIVAN.
teach.b: A line is his if it's in his Divan.
Love the new poem if it helps you. Just don't sign it with his name.

how: Readers who want Hafiz in English look for translations that follow the Persian text of the Divan, often with the Persian alongside, and treat popular modern 'versions' as new poems inspired by him.

o: different printed editions of the same Persian text
early versions of a poem the poet later rewrote

games.q: the real Hafiz and the legend: tap the pairs.
p: the beloved in Hafiz's well-known ghazal
what Hafiz would give for her mole
a new poem under an old poet's name

s: every viral 'Hafiz' poem in English comes from his Divan
some popular ones are modern versions that scholars can't match to the Persian.
Hafiz wrote that he'd give Samarkand and Bukhara for a beloved's mole
it's in his Shirazi Turk ghazal. the meeting with Timur is a later legend.
the Timur meeting is a recorded historical fact
it's a legend; historians doubt the two ever met.

games.q: a wedding planner wants a 'Hafiz' quote for the program. you can find it only in a modern English book, nowhere in the Divan. what's honest?
o: use a real couplet from the Divan, or credit the modern author.
print 'Hafiz'; the guests will never check.
call it 'ancient Persian wisdom' with no name at all.
games.why: a line is Hafiz's if it's in his Divan. a version can be lovely; it just needs its own name.

practice: Take out your phone and find one quote you've saved or shared that's signed Hafiz or Rumi. Look it up against a real edition if you can.
If it isn't there, send the friend who loves it a real couplet from this week, or rename the line kindly: a modern version.

wordCard.voice: Versions: new poems written in a well-known poet's spirit and passed around under his name. Not translations, and not Hafiz.

carryVoice: For the road: not hafiz, said kindly, with the real line ready. Six days into Hafiz.
